tagline.text: A waterfall in Tangalan near Kalibo with seven tiers of limestone pools

location.label: Location
location.text: Barangay Jawili, Tangalan, Aklan (on the coastal road northwest of Kalibo)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–1,200 (per person, day trip round trip from Kalibo including transport, admission and snacks)

children.text: Jawili Falls is a waterfall close to the coast in Tangalan, Aklan, with seven small limestone pools that step down like a staircase. Close to Kalibo and easy to add to a Boracay trip, it can be enjoyed in half a day by combining a swim, a light climb up the steps and neighboring Jawili Beach.
Jawili Falls is in Barangay Jawili, Tangalan, Aklan, in northwestern Panay. Tangalan is a small town about

from the provincial capital Kalibo, on the coastal road from Kalibo toward Caticlan, the gateway to Boracay. The falls consist of seven tiers of limestone pools, so rather than one big drop, the water flows down like stairs. One blog described the height to the top as about 100 feet (about 30 meters), but no official figure was found, so take it as a rough estimate. Tangalan has about 24,000 residents as of the 2024 census and 15 barangays; it was originally a suburb of Makato and became a separate municipality on June 16, 1948 under Republic Act No. 285.

The pools get smaller as you go up, and the dark water stacked step by step over rough limestone is distinctive. According to one visitor's account, some pools are up to about 10 feet (about 3 meters) deep. Children play in the shallow ones, and many people swim in the deeper pools. One guide says shallow and deep areas are mixed, so with children, keep them in the shallow areas and do not dive. Above the falls a stream continues into the forest, and there is shade from the trees.

An oral legend is told about the falls. It appears in travel guides and in writing by a local Aklan author, which say that Inggot and Jawili, siblings (or grandchildren in one version), opened a family keepsake they were told never to open (a purse or a jar), were turned to stone amid thunder and lightning, Jawili's tears became the falls, and Spanish settlers named the place after her. Details (the object, the family relationship) differ by source, but it is given as the origin of the local name and is worth reading with children. The town of Tangalan lists the falls, together with the beach, among tourist spots supported under Project Bugna.

Access is relatively easy. One guide says it is about 30 minutes from Kalibo to Tangalan by jeepney or bus and 10–15 minutes from town to the falls by tricycle. There are huts and rest areas at the entrance, and one blog says the falls and Jawili Beach are about a 5-minute walk apart, though tourists should allow 10–15 minutes. When there is plenty of water the pools look clear, and in the dry season the flow can shrink, so consider the timing. Besides the falls, Tangalan is said to have the Tangalan Marine Sanctuary covering about 375 hectares with a 10-hectare coral garden, so the area suits anyone planning beach and sea activities as well.
Pools made of limestone are layered in seven tiers. The higher you go, the wider the view, and each tier offers a different depth and mood.
The concrete steps to the upper levels are narrow and steep but short. Wet stones are slippery, so wear sandals or sneakers. At the top you can feel the trees and the breeze.
There are shallow pools where children can play and deeper pools good for swimming. Some are said to be as deep as about 10 feet, so check the depth before you get in.
One guide says huts rent for about

, and there are basic restrooms, changing areas and vendors selling snacks. Shops and an information board are at the entrance below the falls. One visitor reports several shops around the falls and a shelter from the rain.
Jawili Beach, a few minutes from the falls, is easy to combine in one trip. One blog says it is about a 5-minute walk to the falls, but tourists should allow 10–15 minutes.
A legend says the siblings Inggot and Jawili turned to stone and that Jawili's tears became the falls. Ask the local signboard or residents for more of the story.
One guide says local guides offer bamboo rafting depending on the season. Check locally on rates and whether it is running.

items.title: Half day from Kalibo
items.subtitle: Combining the falls and the beach

children.text: Take a jeepney or van to Tangalan from the jeepney terminal in downtown Kalibo (about 30–40 minutes).
Get off at the Tangalan public market and take a tricycle to the falls (about 10–15 minutes).
Pay the entrance fee at the entrance and start with the lower pools for a swim.
Climb the concrete steps to see the upper pools and the shade of the forest.
Rent a hut and rest over a packed lunch.
Stop at Jawili Beach by tricycle to see the sea.
Take a jeepney or bus from the Tangalan market back to Kalibo.
In seasons when the sun sets early, going late in the afternoon leaves too little time, so it is best to arrive in the morning.
Leave Boracay for Caticlan Jetty Port and find transport toward Kalibo.
Transfer to public transport from Kalibo to Tangalan, or use a rental car.
Swim at the falls and have lunch at a hut.
See Jawili Beach, then return to Kalibo or Caticlan.
No confirmed source gives specific travel times and fares from Boracay, so check with local transport.
Direct flights run from Manila to Kalibo International Airport (KLO). If you are on a Boracay trip, you can also fly into Caticlan (MPH) and travel toward Kalibo.
From Kalibo Airport to downtown Kalibo, take a taxi or tricycle.
From the Kalibo integrated terminal or the jeepney terminal near the Kalibo public market, take a jeepney, van or bus bound for Tangalan, Ibajay or Nabas. The trip takes about
30–40 minutes
, and the jeepney fare was ₱23 in a 2014 guide and ₱20–50 depending on distance in a 2025 guide, so confirm with the driver (roughly
Get off at the Tangalan public market and take a tricycle or habal-habal to the falls, about
10–15 minutes
One guide also says that renting a van or car in Kalibo takes about
30–45 minutes
One guide says that after leaving Boracay for Caticlan Jetty Port, you follow the coastal road toward Kalibo and reach the falls. One visitor says the falls are easy to miss from this coastal road.
No source gives a specific route, travel time or fare, so check locally.
By public transport, the route through Kalibo is the most common.

The falls are easier to reach in the dry season because of better roads, but according to one visitor, in the dry season the flow can start to dry up. Another guide says the water is clearer and access easier from November to May. The two sources differ somewhat, so if the amount of water matters most, choose just after the rainy season, and if safety and convenience matter most, choose the dry season.
On rainy days the rocks are slippery and the current can be stronger. Weekday mornings are relatively quiet.

There is almost no lodging near the falls, so most people come as a day trip from Kalibo or Boracay. Tangalan has small lodgings, and a few small beach resorts are said to be around Jawili Beach. One blog comment says there are two resorts within walking distance of the falls. Resort names and rates change, so check before booking.

Food at the entrance of the falls is limited to simple shops and stalls. Most accept cash only, so bring small bills, and it is better to bring a packed lunch and water. One guide says waste disposal is limited, so take your trash back with you. For a proper meal, returning to Kalibo gives more choices.

For local information you can contact Tangalan town hall. One guide gives the phone (036) 272 2032 and the email tangalanlgu@gmail.com. For fees, opening hours and group visit rules, the town hall or the signboard at the entrance is the most accurate source. If you combine the falls and the beach in one day, also ask in advance about the last jeepney or bus back to Kalibo.
Bring swimwear, a change of clothes and a towel. One visitor could not get into the water because they were wearing shoes.
Wear aqua shoes or sandals. Wet stones and the concrete steps are slippery.
Pay entrance and hut fees in cash. Bring small bills.
Weekday mornings or early hours are quiet. The sun sets early, so avoid going after 4 PM.
Put your phone in a waterproof pouch, and bring sunscreen, insect repellent and basic first-aid medicine.
Do not dive in shallow water, and always keep an adult close to children.
Do not play loud music, and follow "leave no trace" by taking your trash with you.
On the way back to Kalibo, the easiest way is to take a jeepney or bus from the Tangalan public market. Check the time of the last one in advance.
Even if the water is low in the dry season, combining a walk up to the upper levels with Jawili Beach makes a full half day.
Water depth differs from tier to tier and wet rocks are slippery. In the rainy season and after rain the current gets stronger, so do not get in if it is not safe.
Admission (₱5–40) and opening hours (8 AM–5 PM) differ across sources from 2014 to 2024, so confirm on site.
The height of about 100 feet comes only from a blog's description, and no official figure has been confirmed.
In the dry season the water may shrink and look different. One guide recommends a time when there is more water.
Some sections are narrow, steep steps, so children and older visitors should climb slowly.
No confirmed information is available on travel time and fares from Boracay, so ask locally.
No source says there are lifeguards at the falls. Swimming is at your own risk, so do not go into deep pools alone and keep your belongings where you can see them.
The capital of Aklan and a city with an airport, and the starting point for public transport to Jawili Falls.
A famous beach island reached by boat from Caticlan Jetty Port to the northwest, and a good match for a half-day trip to the falls.
A beach a few minutes from the falls, easy to combine in one trip.
The parish church of St. John Nepomucene, said to have been built in the 1800s, which you can visit in the same town.
